samples.prompt: Write a reflective narrative about revisiting a memory from your youth involving an unfinished or newly constructed building. Describe your philosophical impressions of the empty structure at the time and include a specific incident or action you took during your visit.
samples.generated:
I went back to the <PLACE> and found the new wing still under
construction. I walked round the walls and saw the men digging and
driving and pouring in the concrete. The great tower seemed almost
complete. And when we passed through the gate again there was a
fascinating sense of the newness and the incompleteness of all things.
There were more birds than before; some, like the woodpecker, seemed
to have come especially for this hour of novelty. The air was lighter;
the sky bluer; the whole earth was a new creation. It was the time of
the birds; but it was also, I fancy, the time of the builders. For the
builders are always most hopeful--especially of their own work. I
remember that on the first day of my visit I climbed the steps into the
empty tower. The sun was still out, and I could hear the birds singing
all around me. And then, for some reason that I do not understand, I
began to climb higher and higher. I remember being quite surprised that
I got any further up at all--so many people seem to get so far away in
their cups. But I did get farther up; I got up into the dark upper
chamber; where it seemed impossible to get any further up. I think it
must have been a very dark chamber indeed. When I came down again I was
very glad of the light; though now I feel sure that no bird would ever
have flown into that dark place by accident.

samples.prompt: Write a philosophical essay contrasting two modes of reasoning: one that begins with first principles and fundamental purposes, and another that starts with immediate observations and works backward. Use an extended metaphor involving a common object to illustrate the difference between these approaches.
samples.generated:
The second way is by looking at things as they come; it is like a man
trying to understand a watch by pulling off one piece after another till
he got to the spring. The first method was the only one which the great
religious teachers have ever taken; they begin with some fundamental
principles (such as God) and try to work out all the consequences from
them. But the second method has been adopted by most modern philosophers,
and it is much more difficult to discuss. I would call it the method of
looking at things from below upwards. It is, in short, the method of
seeing things as if you were blind. This is the real meaning of the
famous passage in <PERSON>, where he says that when he looked out of his
window on the dark streets of <PLACE> he saw the city “like a thing
grown up.” And the same phrase applies to many other cases. When I see a
clock I see it growing out of a watch face, and when I see a garden I
see it growing out of a lawn mower or a garden spade. I see the
watch-face growing, not merely as a sort of picture of the stars, but
rather as a growth of stars. Similarly, the trees grow out of a spade, a
wheelbarrow, or even a bicycle, just as a flower grows out of a seed.
In fact, if there were no flowers at all I should still see them
growing. A philosopher who is beginning to understand things must look
at them as if he did not know what they were.
